articles.title: Import once, rebuild everything: why a nightly Apple Health rebuild loses your deltas
articles.excerpt: The nightly rebuild is the pipeline almost everyone writes first. Drop the export, recompute every day from scratch, write it out. It is idempotent, it is easy to reason about, and it quietly throws a…
articles.body: The nightly rebuild is the pipeline almost everyone writes first. Drop the export, recompute every day from scratch, write it out. It is idempotent, it is easy to reason about, and it quietly throws away the one thing a health feed needs: which day changed, and why. The longer version, with the live proof, is on the blog: Import Once, Rebuild Everything . The export is not immutable A full rebuild earns its place. It is stateless: delete the output, re-derive it, and you get the same answer every time. No cache to invalidate, no partial state to repair, no ordering to get wrong. If your export were immutable, it would be the right answer forever. It is not immutable. Late-arriving samples are normal, not an edge case.
articles.author: Philip D'Souza

articles.title: No knee in JPEG quality between 78 and 88, and the cost only jumps above it
articles.excerpt: Is there a knee somewhere between JPEG quality 78 and 88, a point where the next step suddenly stops being worth it? On these 8 samples there is not. Each extra 0.001 of SSIM cost 3.0% to 5.4% more by…
articles.body: Is there a knee somewhere between JPEG quality 78 and 88, a point where the next step suddenly stops being worth it? On these 8 samples there is not. Each extra 0.001 of SSIM cost 3.0% to 5.4% more bytes on photos and 2.9% to 7.5% more on screenshots and text pages across those steps, and the cost only becomes clearly expensive once quality goes above 88. All numbers below come from one run on one Apple-silicon Mac, so read them as "on these samples", not as a rule for every image. How the cost was measured Each sample was a lossless PNG original, encoded to JPEG with Pillow 11.3 (its bundled libjpeg-turbo, 4:2:0 chroma) at quality 70, 75, 78, 80, 84, 88, 92 and 95. SSIM was computed against the lossless original.

articles.title: 4 Types of AI Agent Memory: Profile, Episode, Case, Skill
articles.excerpt: AI agents need more than access to information to handle tasks consistently. They need a way to remember useful details, connect past experiences, and apply what they have learned when a new situation…
articles.body: AI agents need more than access to information to handle tasks consistently. They need a way to remember useful details, connect past experiences, and apply what they have learned when a new situation comes up. A practical way to understand this process is to separate agent memory into four parts: profiles, episodes, cases, and skills. Each type of memory serves a different purpose. Some preserve stable information, while others help agents recall specific events, solve similar problems, or reuse proven steps. Understanding these differences can help us make better decisions about what an AI agent should remember and how that information should be organized. Keep reading to see how the four memory types work together.

articles.title: Flank, flip, or pass: how I coded Reversi in 124 lines for a multiplayer browser game
articles.excerpt: Reversi is one of those games you can explain in a sentence and still lose to for years. Place a disc so that it traps a straight line of your opponent's discs between it and another of yours, and eve…
articles.body: Reversi is one of those games you can explain in a sentence and still lose to for years. Place a disc so that it traps a straight line of your opponent's discs between it and another of yours, and every trapped disc flips to your colour. Whoever owns the most discs when nobody can move wins. On mympgames , my free arcade of 60+ multiplayer browser games, the whole Reversi rule engine is a single 124-line server module. This post walks through it: how the board starts, how a move is checked, the rule about passing that trips up a lot of implementations, and how the client gets just enough information to draw hint dots without doing any rule work itself. The contract every game follows Every game on the site exports the same four things: meta , createState , onAction and publicState .

articles.title: Keeping One Character Consistent Across Short AI Video Clips
articles.excerpt: I've been making short AI video clips for a side project, and the problem that kept tripping me up was the character changing between shots. Hair colour drifts, the jacket changes, the face looks like…
articles.body: I've been making short AI video clips for a side project, and the problem that kept tripping me up was the character changing between shots. Hair colour drifts, the jacket changes, the face looks like a cousin rather than the same person. What helped most was starting from a reference image rather than text alone. With a consistent character ai video workflow, I upload one or two clear pictures of the character and describe only the action and camera move in the prompt. The look stays anchored to the reference, so I can spend the prompt on motion instead of re-describing the outfit every time. A few things I learned along the way: Use a reference with a plain background and good, even lighting. Busy backgrounds leak into every shot. Keep the prompt short: subject, action, camera, mood.

articles.title: Stopping a Website AI Chat Agent From Making Things Up
articles.excerpt: A website chat agent that answers most questions well and invents a refund policy once a week is worse than no chat agent. The visitor screenshots the wrong answer, and now your support team has to ho…
articles.body: A website chat agent that answers most questions well and invents a refund policy once a week is worse than no chat agent. The visitor screenshots the wrong answer, and now your support team has to honor it or argue about it. Picking a better model doesn't fix this. Four boring layers do: what the agent is allowed to read, what it is told never to say, what it is allowed to do, and who reads the transcripts afterwards. Here is how we set up each one. 1. A knowledge base someone actually reviewed Most bad answers come from bad source material, not from the model. The usual mistake is pointing the agent at the whole website and a folder of old PDFs. That folder holds the 2023 price list, a promo that ended, and three versions of the cancellation policy.

articles.excerpt: From Russian masterpieces to modern dystopias, these are the books that never get old.
articles.body: Most of us treat classic literature like a checklist to conquer in high school or college and then never touch those books again. You power through the plot, underline a few quotes for a term paper, and move on to whatever else is new. The catch is that great books rarely reveal their most fascinating tricks on the first pass. When you already know the ending, your brain stops racing for answers and begins to notice the machinery holding all those mysteries and themes together. articles.body: The December full moon reaches peak illumination at 8:28 p.m. EST on Dec. 23 (0128 GMT on Dec. 24) as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. It is often called the "Cold Moon" in reference to the frigid temperatures that prevail in the Northern Hemisphere around the time of its rising, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . December's full moon will also occur close to perigee — the moon's closest point to Earth in its elliptical orbit — giving rise to a spectacular supermoon. A supermoon can appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than a full moon at its farthest point from Earth (also known as a micromoon)..

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 25, 1970: NASA's 'wingless' M2-F3 'lifting body' aircraft makes its 1st powered flight ahead of supersonic tests
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight. The M2-F3 aircraft was a heavyweight "lifting body" designed to test its ability to produce most of its lift through its fuselage instead of wings. It's commonly referred to as a "wingless" aircraft. After Air Force test pilot Bill Dana took the M2-F3 on three unpowered glide test flights, he did the first powered flight, too. Dana soared to an altitude of 45,000 feet during this flight, which lasted just over 6 minutes. He didn't break the sound barrier this time, but he did on later flights. The M2-F3 flew a total of 27 missions in its three-year flight history. Its top speed was 1.6 times the speed of sound, and its top altitude was 71,500 feet.
